title: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective ×a×b for multiplicative semigroups mod q
connection: BLMV give effective equidistribution of orbits of the multiplicative semigroup ⟨a,b⟩ acting on ℤ/q (Furstenberg ×2×3 discrete analogue); ES e-slices ask whether −1 lies in a product set built from a few multiplicative generators mod e.
why: Shows when a 2-generator multiplicative semigroup fills (ℤ/q)^× — the 'enough generators' threshold relevant to pooling slices.
first_step: Compute, for e-slices at hard primes, the size of the semigroup generated by the two smallest prime factors of N mod e.
refs: Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh, Some effective results for ×a×b, Ergodic Theory Dynam. Systems 29 (2009)

title: Tao's Collatz 'almost bounded orbits' technique for greedy-with-choice Egyptian algorithms
connection: Tao (2019) analysed a 3-adic Syracuse random variable to show almost all Collatz orbits attain almost bounded values; ES solutions are produced by greedy-type algorithms (choose x ≈ n/4, recurse on the remainder) whose residue dynamics resemble Syracuse.
why: A stabilisation argument for the remainder's residue distribution could show 'greedy with bounded look-ahead succeeds for almost all n in log density' — and identify the structure of failures.
first_step: Implement the greedy-with-choice algorithm (x = ⌈n/4⌉ + k, k ≤ K) and record the residue distribution of remainders at each step for p ≤ 10^7.
refs: Tao, Almost all orbits of the Collatz map attain almost bounded values, Forum Math. Pi 10 (2022), arXiv:1909.03562

title: Host–Kra / Frantzikinakis ergodic structure for multiplicative ES colourings
connection: Host–Kra factors describe multiple ergodic averages; Frantzikinakis–Host apply them to multiplicative functions; the colouring of n by 'ES shape type' is multiplicatively closed (solutions lift to multiples).
why: A Furstenberg-correspondence model of the ES shape colouring could show forced configurations in each colour class.
first_step: Define the colouring n ↦ (minimal certificate type) and test partition-regularity-type configurations numerically.
refs: Host–Kra, Nonconventional ergodic averages and nilmanifolds, Ann. Math. 161 (2005)

title: Spanning-tree values and Zaremba (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak) applied to fan graphs
connection: Chan–Kontorovich–Pak prove exponential growth of the set of spanning-tree counts of n-vertex planar graphs via continued fractions, thin orbits and Zaremba. ES₅ asks the same kind of question for continuants of length 3 with a sign condition.
why: It is the nearest proved theorem in which spanning-tree counts and continued fractions are linked through thin-orbit methods. Their graphs realise numerators of CFs, as our fan does for HJ length 3.
first_step: Read arXiv:2411.18782 §2 (graph ↔ CF dictionary). Check whether their construction realises a prescribed numerator p with a prescribed denominator class (A/p) = −1 at bounded length.
refs: arXiv:2411.18782 (Chan–Kontorovich–Pak, Spanning trees and continued fractions)

title: Cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A) with a 3-curve resolution and non-residue A
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] is the minimal resolution chain (−v,−t,−u) of the cyclic quotient singularity 1/p(1,A). ES₅(p) ⇔ some 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has exactly 3 exceptional curves.
why: Singularity theory controls resolution lengths via Riemenschneider duality, P-resolutions and smoothing components (KSB). The ES sign is a Galois-type datum: is 1/p(1,A) isomorphic over a quadratic twist to 1/p(1,1)?
first_step: Compute embedding dimension and Riemenschneider dual lengths for A ∈ L₃(p); test whether the dual-chain length distribution differs between (A/p) = ±1.

title: Frobenius-class form: uv | n+u+v ⇔ n is in the 'Frobenius shadow' of the numerical semigroup ⟨u,v⟩
connection: n = tuv−u−v ⇔ n ≡ −(u+v) (mod uv). If gcd(u,v) = 1 (automatic for interior words at a prime n), Popoviciu's formula gives exactly t−1 representations of n as au+bv (a,b ≥ 0), and uv−u−v is the Frobenius number. Without coprimality this fails (t = u = v = 2, n = 4). ES₅ words are pairs (u,v) whose denumerant at n is in the Frobenius residue class, plus a sign condition.
why: The theory of numerical semigroups and denumerants (Popoviciu, Sylvester, Ramírez Alfonsín) gives a new vocabulary for the forest F_p (uv | p+u+v), with generating-function tools.
first_step: Express the ES₅ sign in terms of (u,v,n) via denumerant data; check whether Σ_{(u,v)} sign·q^n has a Popoviciu-type generating function (∏ 1/(1−q^u)(1−q^v) restricted to a class).
refs: Ramírez Alfonsín, The Diophantine Frobenius Problem (2005)

title: Christoffel/Sturmian word of slope A/p with three runs
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is a run-length statistic of the Christoffel word of slope A/p (equivalently the cutting sequence of the segment to (p,A)). ES₅ asks for a non-residue A whose Christoffel word has the minimal 3-block structure.
why: Combinatorics on words has exact results on Christoffel words, palindromes and standard factorizations, which might give explicit constructions of A with prescribed structure, for instance via palindromic closure.
first_step: Express r(p/A) = 3 as a factorisation condition on the Christoffel word; test whether the Lothaire standard factorisation relates the two halves to (A/p).
refs: Lothaire, Algebraic Combinatorics on Words, ch. 2

title: Plumbing calculus moves (blow-up/blow-down of ±1 curves) as certificate transport
connection: Kirby calculus moves change a plumbing chain without changing the boundary lens space. The boundary words (letters = 1) of LENGTH_THREE are formal words that become interior after blow-downs.
why: This gives a topological interpretation of the repo's boundary/interior word distinction and of 'transport' moves between certificates (boundary-preserving blow-ups do not change |det|, so transport between different n needs a non-boundary-preserving move such as a surgery/cobordism step; identify which).
first_step: Map LENGTH_THREE formal words (letter 1) to blow-down sequences; check whether ES transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md) are Kirby moves.

title: Farey-graph geodesic of length 3 in the non-residue class
connection: HJ length r(p/A) is (up to normalisation) a combinatorial distance-type statistic in the Farey graph from ∞ to p/A via a specific path type. ES₅ asks whether the Farey ball of 'HJ radius 3' around ∞ contains a vertex p/A with A a QNR.
why: The Farey graph is hyperbolic geometry's combinatorial skeleton, and its metric theory (Beardon–Hockman–Short) is well developed.
first_step: Compare r(p/A) with Farey distance d(∞, p/A) for p < 10⁴; check whether the ES₅ condition is a Farey-distance condition for a known metric.

title: Lyness 5-cycle with a coefficient: integrable map whose integer orbits are ES₅ words
connection: The pentagon Ptolemy relations with one frozen side N give a period-5 birational map (a Lyness-type recurrence x_{k+1}x_{k−1} = x_k + c_k with c ∈ {1,N}). Integer orbits are words. Lyness maps have an invariant cubic (elliptic) fibration.
why: Discrete integrable systems give invariants and elliptic fibrations of such maps; the invariant of the coefficient-N Lyness cycle gives each word a 'conserved energy', possibly with arithmetic meaning.
first_step: Compute the invariant rational function of the (1,1,1,1,N) Lyness cycle (sympy). Evaluate it on words and look for a link with the sign or with t.

title: Backward-CF (Rényi-type) map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x: infinite invariant measure and orbit length 3
connection: The HJ expansion is generated by a backward-CF (Rényi-type) map with an infinite invariant measure (parabolic fixed point). The coordinate convention matters: in the variable x = A/p the map T(x) = ⌈1/x⌉ − 1/x reproduces the HJ step, whereas the map x ↦ 1/(1−x) − ⌊⋯⌋ started at A/p does not (5/17 takes 4 steps, but its HJ length is 3). Short orbits to 0 in 3 steps are the ES₅ words.
why: Infinite-ergodic-theory tools (Aaronson, Thaler) describe return statistics near the parabolic point, and ES words are 'fast escapes', the complementary regime.
first_step: Compute the measure of points with exactly 3-step Rényi orbits to the cusp at resolution 1/p; compare with |L₃(p)|/p.
refs: Aaronson, An Introduction to Infinite Ergodic Theory (1997)

title: Mayer/Gauss–Kuzmin–Wirsing transfer operator twisted by (·/p): spectral gap for character sums over CF sets
connection: Character sums over sets defined by CF conditions can be studied by transfer operators with a character twist (as in Bourgain–Kontorovich and Dolgopyat). A spectral gap gives cancellation in Σ_{A: CF condition} χ(A).
why: It is the native way to get cancellation for CF-defined sets, but works for growing lengths, not length 3. Recorded as the nearest tool.
first_step: Record the length threshold L(p) beyond which twisted transfer-operator methods give non-trivial Σ_{A ∈ S_L(p)} (A/p); compare with λ(p) data.
refs: Mayer 1991 (transfer operator of the Gauss map)

title: Hilbert modular / Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles for the pair (A, A*) with AA* = tp+1
connection: Hirzebruch–Zagier cycles T_N on Hilbert modular surfaces have intersection numbers given by class numbers. Pairs (A,A*) with AA* = tp + 1 are points of a 'norm' condition that might be intersection points of T_N with a modular curve.
why: Hirzebruch–Zagier gives exact intersection numbers as coefficients of modular forms; if certificates are intersection points, their count is a known modular coefficient.
first_step: Check whether pairs (A, A*) with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t) and AA* = tp+1 are naturally CM points / intersection points on X(1) × X(1) (i.e. on a Hecke correspondence T_{tp+1}).
refs: Hirzebruch–Zagier, Intersection numbers of curves on Hilbert modular surfaces (Invent. 1976)

title: Quadratic residue codes: ES₅ failure as S₃(p) ⊂ support of the QR idempotent
connection: The QR code of length p is defined by the QR set. ES₅ fails at p iff S₃(p) ⊆ QR. Coding theory studies which structured sets sit inside QR (e.g. minimum-weight words, automorphism group PSL₂(p) acting on QR codes).
why: The QR code's automorphism group PSL₂(F_p) is large. Words (as SL₂ data) act naturally, so S₃(p) ⊆ QR might be translated into a code-automorphism statement.
first_step: Check whether S₃(p) is a union of orbits of some subgroup of PSL₂(F_p) stabilising QR; if so, failure would be forced or forbidden group-theoretically.
refs: MacWilliams–Sloane, The Theory of Error-Correcting Codes, ch. 16

title: Gauss-sum / Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃(p)} at the quadratic character
connection: ES₅(p) ⇔ Σ_{A ∈ S₃(p)} (A/p) < |S₃(p)|. In coding/Fourier terms, the quadratic Fourier coefficient of 1_{S₃} must not be maximal. Uncertainty principles (Tao's prime-field uncertainty, Biró–Meshulam) bound how concentrated a set and its Fourier transform can be.
why: Tao's uncertainty principle for F_p says |supp f| + |supp f̂| ≥ p + 1. Indicator sets that are subsets of QR have structured Fourier transforms, which gives a potential contradiction with S₃'s known Fourier structure.
first_step: Compute the Fourier transform of 1_{S₃(p)} for p < 5000; check whether 'S₃ ⊆ QR' would force a Fourier property contradicted by S₃'s divisor structure.
refs: Tao, An uncertainty principle for cyclic groups of prime order (MRL 2005)

title: Stern's diatomic sequence: (p, A) = (s(k), s(k+1)) and HJ length as a binary-run statistic of k
connection: Every coprime pair occurs exactly once as consecutive Stern values, and the CF of p/A is encoded by the run lengths of k's binary expansion. ES₅ ⇔ some k with s(k) = p, s(k±1) ≡ non-residue, and k's binary word in a 3-run HJ pattern.
why: This makes ES₅ a statement about binary words, so automata/regular-language tools (automatic sequences, Stern's sequence is 2-regular) apply.
first_step: Find the exact HJ-run encoding (LORENZINI_W §7 has a Stern coding); enumerate k with ≤ 3 HJ-runs and s(k) = p, check the sign.

title: Hilbert basis of a 2-dimensional cone: ES₅ ⇔ a cone of index p in the non-residue class with a 5-element Hilbert basis
connection: The Hilbert basis of cone((0,1),(p,−A)) consists of the HJ convergents, so it has r(p/A) + 2 elements. ES₅ ⇔ some cone of type 1/p(1,A) with (A/p) = −1 has Hilbert basis of size 5.
why: Integer-programming/commutative-algebra native: Hilbert-basis sizes and normal semigroup rings (embedding dimension). Toric-ideal theory gives explicit invariants.
first_step: Compute the semigroup-ring invariants (Hilbert series, a-invariant) of the 5-element cones and test whether the sign is a ring-theoretic invariant (e.g. class group element of the toric ring).

title: Hecke (Rosen) continued fractions: ES-type statements for Hecke triangle groups G_q
connection: Replace SL₂(ℤ) by the Hecke group G_q and HJ fractions by Rosen λ_q-fractions. 'Every element of a cusp set has a length-3 expansion with a character condition' becomes a family of ES-analogues indexed by q.
why: Some Hecke groups are arithmetic (q = 3, 4, 6) and others non-arithmetic. Comparing ES analogues across them separates arithmetic from combinatorial ingredients.
first_step: Define the λ₄-analogue (G₄ is commensurable with Γ₀(2)) of words and check whether a T1-type obstruction occurs.
refs: Rosen, A class of continued fractions associated with certain properly discontinuous groups (Duke 1954)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Fermionic/spin TQFT: the parity condition '4 divides an entry' as a spin-structure obstruction
connection: In 3-manifold topology, spin structures on L(p,q) and plumbings are tracked by characteristic sublinks (Wu sets). 'Some pentagon entry ≡ 0 (mod 4)' may say the plumbing admits a spin structure with a given Rokhlin invariant mod 16.
why: Rokhlin's theorem (σ ≡ 0 mod 16 for spin closed 4-manifolds) is a rigid integrality statement. If the ES sign is a Rokhlin invariant, T1 might be a Rokhlin-type obstruction.
first_step: Compute μ-invariants (Neumann–Siebenmann) of L(p,A) via plumbing for all words with p < 500 and compare with the sign.
refs: Neumann, An invariant of plumbed homology spheres (1980)

title: Integrable billiards / Sturmian cutting sequences of slope A/p in a square
connection: A billiard trajectory in the unit square with slope A/p has a cutting sequence (Sturmian/Christoffel word). HJ length is a renormalisation depth (number of Rauzy–Veech-type induction steps of a specific kind).
why: Rauzy–Veech induction is the dynamics-native renormalisation, and it has a version for square-tiled surfaces where arithmetic data (p) enters as the number of squares.
first_step: Identify HJ steps with a renormalisation algorithm on the square torus; check whether a square-tiled surface with p squares realises words as cylinder decompositions.

title: Zolotarev: (A/p) = sign of the permutation x ↦ Ax on ℤ/p — ES₅ as 'an odd multiplication permutation with a length-3 HJ structure'
connection: (A/p) = sgn(π_A), π_A(x) = Ax mod p. ES₅(p) ⇔ some A ∈ L₃(p) gives an odd permutation. Permutation-group language: the parity of π_A can be computed from the cycle type (order of A in F_p^*).
why: (A/p) = −1 ⇔ ord(A) is even with the full 2-part of p−1, i.e. A generates the 2-Sylow quotient. So ES₅ becomes a statement about the 2-adic valuation of multiplicative orders of elements of L₃(p).
first_step: For p ≡ 1 (8), compute v₂(ord_p(A)) for A ∈ L₃(p); ES₅ ⇔ some A has v₂(ord A) = v₂(p−1). Look at the distribution of v₂(ord A) on words.

title: Fixed-letter word families as Chebotarev sets: density of p covered by words with (t,u) fixed
connection: Fixing (t,u) makes A = tu − 1 fixed, and the word exists iff v = (p+u)/A is an integer, i.e. p ≡ −u (mod A). The sign condition (A/p) = −1 is then fixed by reciprocity together with the 2-adic supplement when A is even: given p ≡ −u (mod A) and p mod 4 (and mod 8 if A is even), (A/p) = ±(−u/A) is determined. So each fixed (t,u) covers either a whole residue class mod 4A of primes or nothing (that is, it is the Mordell/B1 structure).
why: It is the cleanest 'fixed-menu' native form, and B1 says finitely many never suffice. The densities and their union bound give the exact covering deficit in Chebotarev language.
first_step: Compute the union density of fixed-(t,u) families with tu ≤ T as T grows (inclusion–exclusion via CRT), and the rate at which the uncovered density decays.

title: Torus bundles T_{γ_w}: H₁ order |tr γ_w − 2| and Anosov dynamics
connection: The mapping torus of γ_w on T² has H₁ = ℤ ⊕ coker(γ_w − I) with |coker| = |tr γ_w − 2| = tu + tv − 4. Its linking form and Sol geometry are explicit.
why: A 3-manifold carrier where the trace, not p, is the order. The ES sign may appear as a linking-form class at a different modulus, which gives a new dictionary for transport between p and traces.
first_step: Compute the linking form of T_{γ_w} for words at p < 300 and look for a relation between its square class and (A/p).

title: Integer matrices with prescribed characteristic polynomial: ES words as conjugacy classes
connection: Words correspond to γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ) with b = p and a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c). Counting SL₂(ℤ) matrices with given trace and a fixed entry is a classical problem (Eskin–McMullen counting in affine symmetric varieties).
why: Eskin–McMullen/Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak give asymptotic counts in growing balls, which shows the shape of the main term but with no fixed-p pointwise content (B3).
first_step: Note calibration; compute the count of γ with b = p and trace ≤ T as T grows, and its sign-weighted version.
refs: Eskin–McMullen, Mixing, counting, and equidistribution in Lie groups (Duke 1993)

title: Integral points on the 'word variety' as an affine homogeneous space under a unipotent group
connection: {γ ∈ SL₂ : b = p} is preserved by left and right multiplication by lower unipotents [[1,0],[k,1]] (left multiplication shifts d by kp, right multiplication shifts a by kp). Words are the integral points with level-structure congruences in a bounded region.
why: Homogeneous-space integral points with congruence conditions are governed by strong approximation (here for a unipotent group, which is trivial) and by the box. This explains why only the archimedean box matters.
first_step: Record: strong approximation for the unipotent group is automatic, so all ES₅ content is in the archimedean box (positivity, sizes). Use as a calibration item for future 'group-action' proposals.

title: Fourier–Dedekind sums / Beck–Robins: lattice points in the word region via Dedekind–Rademacher sums
connection: Counting lattice points in rational polytopes yields Fourier–Dedekind sums (Beck–Robins). The ES₅ sign involves Dedekind sums (DEDEKIND_ES). Combining the two might express Σ_{words} (sign) as a finite combination of Dedekind–Rademacher sums.
why: Dedekind–Rademacher sums satisfy reciprocity laws that allow fast evaluation and sometimes positivity statements.
first_step: Express |L₃(p)| and Σ (A/p) for p < 1000 in terms of Dedekind–Rademacher sums r_n(a,b;c) by linear fitting; look for exact identities.

title: Continued fraction of √f, f = μ² − n: Lagrange's |value| < 2√f and V_n points among convergents
connection: Small values of an indefinite binary form occur at convergents of its roots (Lagrange: |Q(A,B)| < 2√f/… ⇒ (B,A) is a convergent-type pair). V_n points with small D are therefore convergents of (μ ± √f)/n.
why: This makes V_n points a CF computation, with period-length and Pell-unit structure, and connects to ES's other CF forms (HJ length).
first_step: Verify that every V_n point at μ with D < √f comes from a convergent of (μ + √f)/n; then express the B = 1 condition as a condition on the convergent index.

title: Semigroup orbit counting (Bourgain–Kontorovich, Kontorovich–Oh) for the ES word semigroup with entry p
connection: QUESTION_R casts words as elements of a semigroup Ψ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ)_{≥0}. Thin-orbit counting with congruence conditions gives asymptotic counts of orbit elements with entry ≤ N in progressions (level of distribution).
why: This gives averaged ES₅ results with power savings, and RS's local–global theorem shows that for fat semigroups the sporadic set is finite. The ES semigroup's exponent δ decides which regime applies.
first_step: Compute the critical exponent δ of the semigroup generated by the word letters (likely 1, i.e. not thin). If δ = 1, record that RS-type local–global for 'fat' semigroups is the relevant theorem class.

title: Heilbronn's average CF length with a quadratic-character twist
connection: Heilbronn: the average number of steps of the Euclidean algorithm on a/p is (12 log 2/π²) log p. Twisting by (a/p), the difference between average lengths over QR and QNR a is a 'character-correlated CF statistic'.
why: If QNRs have systematically shorter/longer expansions (in HJ form), that is a global bias relevant to λ(p) ≤ 3. Twisted Heilbronn sums reduce to Kloosterman-type sums (Ustinov's methods).
first_step: Caveat from a cheap test (scripts/z52b_translate_cheap.py, p < 3000): the plain mean of HJ length is dominated by a near p (p/(p−1) = [[2,…,2]] has length p−1, and (−1/p) = 1 puts it in QR), so QR − QNR mean differences are large noise (0.2 to 9.7). Use regular-CF length, log-HJ length or the count of A with r(p/A) ≤ L instead, for p < 10⁵.
refs: Ustinov, on statistical properties of finite continued fractions (check)

title: Gauss composition of the word forms: is there a group law on words of fixed level t?
connection: Words of level t correspond to factorisations N_t = A·A* with A ≡ A* ≡ −1 (mod t), i.e. to ideal-like objects. If they correspond to ideals in an order (e.g. of disc −4t or t² − 4), composition may combine words of p₁ and p₂ into words of p₁p₂-related N.
why: A composition law gives a multiplicative structure on certificates, the missing 'algebraic rigidity' (R-type) in FRONTIER's meta-finding.
first_step: Test: given words of level t at n₁ and n₂, is there a natural word of level t at some n₃ = f(n₁,n₂) (e.g. via (tn₁+1)(tn₂+1) = t·n₃ + 1 with n₃ = tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂)? Check sign multiplicativity.

title: The multiplicative monoid (tn₁+1)(tn₂+1) = t(tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂) + 1: ES₅ transport n₁ ⋆_t n₂
connection: The set {N : N ≡ 1 (mod t)} is a multiplicative monoid, and n ↦ tn + 1 transports the operation n₁ ⋆ n₂ = tn₁n₂ + n₁ + n₂. Words of level t at n₁ and n₂ give factorisations whose products are factorisations of N(n₁ ⋆ n₂) with factors ≡ 1 (mod t), not −1. Mixing parities yields −1 classes.
why: It is an explicit transport law candidate: ES₅ data at n₁, n₂ might produce data at n₁ ⋆_t n₂. Iterated, the failure set must be closed under the inverse operation.
first_step: Compute: from words (A₁, A₁*) at n₁ and (A₂, A₂*) at n₂, does A₁A₂* (≡ +1 mod t) or A₁·(something) give a valid word at n₁ ⋆ n₂? Check by brute force for small n.

title: Pell-like recurrence: words at p from words at smaller primes via SL₂ conjugation by a fixed matrix
connection: Conjugating γ_w by a fixed S ∈ SL₂(ℤ) preserves trace but moves the entry p to a new value b′ = linear in (a,b,c,d). Integer orbits of the conjugation action on {γ with b prime} are Pell-like recurrences relating words of different primes.
why: It gives transport laws with group structure (like Vieta jumping). If a recurrence preserves the sign and sizes, failures would propagate along orbits.
first_step: For S = [[1,1],[0,1]] and [[1,0],[1,1]], compute how words transform (when the image is a word) and how the sign changes.

title: Cohn matrices / Markov-tree calculus for products M(v)M(t)M(u)
connection: Markov numbers are entries of Cohn matrices, i.e. products of two generators along the Markov tree, and Christoffel words index them. ES words are length-3 products in the HJ generators. Cohn's calculus (trace identities, Fricke relations tr(AB) + tr(AB⁻¹) = tr A tr B) gives algebraic relations among such products.
why: Fricke trace identities make the Markoff equation appear from SL₂ traces. A trace-identity derivation of S_{n,D} from words would unify MARKOFF_ES and the HJ forms.
first_step: Compute tr(M(v)M(t)M(u)) and Fricke-related traces of pairs of word matrices; search for the relation nA² + B² + D = ABC among them.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Meta: the chain matrix M(t,u,v) as a common carrier in ≥ 8 fields — a transfer table of nearest theorems
connection: M(t,u,v) is simultaneously a reduced Laplacian, an electrical network, a ternary Gram matrix, a plumbing intersection form, a cyclic-quotient resolution graph, a FQH K-matrix, an A₂ frieze with coefficient and an SL₂ word. For each field, record the strongest pointwise existence theorem about this object.
why: It organises the translation work so that a single new theorem in one field can be checked for transfer to all others.
first_step: Build the table (field, object, nearest pointwise theorem, what it would need) from items in this lane; mark empty cells as targets.

title: Riemenschneider point diagram: dual chains and the sign under p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: The Riemenschneider dual of p/A is p/(p − A), and (p−A/p) = (A/p) for p ≡ 1 (4). Duality maps length-3 chains (v,t,u) to chains of length v + t + u − 5. So ES₅ is also a statement about QNR fractions whose dual chain has a specific long shape.
why: The dual picture (long chains of 2's and a few larger entries) is where Zaremba-type 'bounded digits' tools live. ES₅ becomes 'some QNR has a dual with ≤ 3 non-2 blocks'.
first_step: Express ES₅ via the dual: QNR B with p/B = [[2,…,2, a, 2,…,2, b, 2,…]] of a specific block shape; count such B via digit-structure.

title: Frobenius number analogue for three generators: n = tuv − u − v as a three-generator semigroup statistic?
connection: For coprime u, v, uv − u − v is the Frobenius number of ⟨u,v⟩. For three generators there are formulas (e.g. for ⟨u, v, w⟩ with structure, Rødseth). Is tuv − u − v the Frobenius number of a natural 3-generated semigroup (for instance ⟨u, v, tuv⟩ is trivial)? If so, I3 becomes 'every large n is a Frobenius number of a semigroup of a given shape'.
why: 'Which integers are Frobenius numbers of 3-generated semigroups' is a studied question; a match would bring that literature in.
first_step: Search small cases: for given n = tuv − u − v, compute Frobenius numbers of ⟨a,b,c⟩ with a,b,c ≤ 50 and test whether some natural family reproduces tuv − u − v.

title: Conjugacy classes in SL₂(ℤ/4) and the slot lemma: '4 divides a pentagon entry' as a class condition on γ_w mod 4
connection: The slot lemma is a mod-4 condition on (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. on γ_w mod 4 together with the frieze. SL₂(ℤ/4) has order 48; the sign may be a class function on SL₂(ℤ/4) restricted to word images.
why: A class-function description would let representation theory of the finite group SL₂(ℤ/4) (and its Weil representation) organise all sign computations.
first_step: Tabulate γ_w mod 4 and mod 8 for all words of p < 10⁴; check whether the sign is a function of the conjugacy class (or of the double coset) mod 4 or 8.

title: Additive energy / multiplicative energy of the word set and character-sum bounds via energy
connection: Bounds for Σ_{A∈S} χ(A) over a set S follow from its multiplicative energy E(S) (Shkredov, Chang). S₃(p) is small (log²p), so energy bounds are trivial, but over the union ∪_{L ≤ L₀} S_L(p) the energy might be small enough.
why: It is the native additive-combinatorics route to non-trivial character sums over thin sets, and it pins down the minimal L where energy methods start working.
first_step: Compute the multiplicative energy of S_L(p) for L ≤ 6 and p ~ 10⁵; find the least L where E(S_L) ≪ |S_L|³/p^δ.

title: Integral Apollonian-type packing whose curvatures are ES-word data
connection: Apollonian packings have curvature quadruples satisfying Descartes's equation. A packing or a thin-group orbit whose curvatures include p exactly when ES₅(p) holds would put ES in the Apollonian local-global framework (where reciprocity obstructions are understood).
why: Speculative construction target; QUESTION_R and apollonian_reciprocity explored nearby ideas.
first_step: Look for a quadratic form F (Descartes-like, signature (3,1) or (2,1)) and a thin orbit whose entries realise (t,u,v)-data with p as a coordinate.

title: Global by-excess (HJ) tree of all length-3 pairs and the forest colouring
connection: The HJ algorithm acts on pairs: (p, A) → (A, u) → (u, 1) → (1, 0) for p/A = [[v,t,u]] (A = tu − 1, vA − p = u). Reading it backwards, all pairs (m, a) of HJ length 3, over all m, form level 3 of one global tree rooted at (1, 0) (a Stern–Brocot-type tree for the by-excess algorithm). Mod p, u ≡ vA, which recovers (A/p) = (uv/p), the forest colouring.
why: It places all words for all p in one tree, so that the ES₅ question 'level-3 node with first coordinate p and QNR colour' becomes a tree-colouring question across p. Tree statistics such as the number of level-3 nodes with first coordinate m (≍ log²m) are explicit.
first_step: Generate the level-3 layer of the global tree for m < 10⁶; for each prime m record the colours; look for inherited colour patterns from level-2 parents (u,1) → (tu−1, u) that are independent of m.

title: Continued-fraction periodicity vs. ES₅ length: Lagrange's proof structure
connection: Pell's solution comes from the periodic CF of √D. ES₅ ⟺ λ(p) ≤ 3 (a continued-fraction length condition for rationals with denominator p). Look for a quadratic irrational (depending on p) whose CF period contains an ES₅ witness, so periodicity forces existence.
why: Odd but concrete: links ES₅'s CF-length formulation to the one every-n theorem driven by CF structure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compute the CF periods of √p, √(4p+1), (1+√p)/2 and check whether an ES₅ witness can be read off from convergents.

title: Product of three sets in SL₂(ℤ): ES words as A·T·A with entry p
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd/Helfgott growth makes products of a few sets fill SL₂(F_q). ES words p = tuv − u − v are length-3 'minus continuants': the (1,1) entry of M(u)M(t)M(v) with M(a) = [[a,−1],[1,0]]. ES ⟺ some product in A·T·A (with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has the right entry.
why: Places ES in the product-set/growth framework where 'every element' theorems exist (at least modulo q).
first_step: Check numerically how the (1,1)-entries of M(u)M(t)M(v), u,v,t ≤ X, distribute modulo small q and whether all residues are hit with the expected frequency (local), then compare with the archimedean count.

title: Modular-Zaremba + size control: words with (1,2)-entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and size < 2p
connection: Moshchevitin–Shkredov solve a modular Zaremba problem by growth in SL₂(F_p). ES words: length-3 minus-continuant products; require the relevant entry ≡ 0 (mod p) and bounded by 2p, forcing equality with p. Equidistribution mod p of entries of words of archimedean size ≤ p is the needed input.
why: Separates ES into a modular part (growth, potentially 'every p') and a size part (counting words in a box).
first_step: Numerically test equidistribution mod p of the entries of length-3 words with entries ≤ p (count ≈ p log p) for p ~ 10⁶; measure deviations at 0 mod p.

title: Niederreiter's recursive constructions for prime powers → ES exponential families
connection: Niederreiter proved Zaremba for every power of 2, 3, 5 by explicit recursive constructions. The repo proved ES for 3·2^s + 1, 7·4^s + 9, 63·2^s + 1; open: 15·2^s + 1, 4^s + 297. Import the recursive (q → 2q, q → 3q) construction idea: produce certificates at n_{s+1} from those at n_s.
why: Recursive constructions along exponential families are the only way Zaremba got 'every member' for infinite families.
first_step: For 15·2^s + 1, list known certificates for s ≤ 60 and look for a recursion (u,B,C)_s → (u,B,C)_{s+k}.

title: Counting integral points on the quadric ad − pc = 1 (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak / Eskin–McMullen)
connection: Oppenheim/Margulis and DRS/EM count integral points on affine homogeneous varieties via dynamics. The SL₂ form of ES: integer points of the affine quadric ad − pc = 1 (degenerate as a ternary quadratic polynomial: quadratic part ad of rank 2, linear in c — a family of hyperbolas ad = 1 + pc) with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c), c ∈ 4ℕ, a, d ≥ 1. Decompose by c into congruence-subgroup cosets and count each via mixing.
why: Homogeneous-dynamics counts are pointwise in the variety (here: in p), unlike sieve averages.
first_step: For fixed c, the conditions define a coset of a congruence subgroup; compute the expected count Σ_c vol(coset ∩ region) and compare with R(p).

title: Shrinking-target property for every closed horocycle
connection: Logarithm laws (Kleinbock–Margulis) give deep excursions for almost every orbit; ES would need them for the specific closed horocycle of length p and depth ~ p^{θ}. Tseng (Math. Z. 2022) proves shrinking-cusp-target equidistribution for long closed horocycles (effective version included).
why: If a deep-excursion theorem for every closed horocycle exists at depth p^{θ}, the CF-length formulation might follow for a range of shapes.
first_step: Read Tseng, 'Shrinking target equidistribution of horocycles in cusps', Math. Z. 302 (2022), arXiv:2106.00836, and Kelmer, Israel J. Math. 229 (2019), arXiv:1708.08953 (both verified to exist); extract the deepest cusp target reachable for a closed horocycle of length p.

title: Monotone-quantity flow on certificate space
connection: Perelman finished Poincaré with a flow and monotone entropy that forces termination at a canonical object. ES: define a deterministic 'flow' on candidate triples (x, y, z) for 4/p (e.g. a descent on the defect 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) using local moves) with a monovariant that can only stop at a certificate, and prove no other stopping states exist (or classify them).
why: Odd but concrete: a local-move dynamical system on integer triples is easy to experiment with; classification of its sinks is a finite-ish problem per p.
first_step: Design local moves (change one coordinate by ±1, or by divisor-jumps) decreasing |defect| and compute sinks for p ≤ 10⁴.
refs: arXiv:math/0211159 (Perelman, The entropy formula for the Ricci flow)

title: Critical exponent of the ES word set on the Bourgain–Kontorovich dimension scale
connection: BK's density-one Zaremba needs the Hausdorff dimension of the bounded-quotient Cantor set above 5/6 (positive proportion above 1/2, etc.). The ES word set (minus-continuants of length 3 with t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p)) has #words ≤ X ≈ X log X; compute its effective 'critical exponent' and where it sits relative to BK thresholds.
why: Places ES in the thin-orbit hierarchy: it is 'fat' (exponent 1 with log), explaining density one, and shows the every-p question is about the log factor.
first_step: Count ES words ≤ X for X up to 10⁹ and fit X^δ (log X)^a; compare with the semigroup Hausdorff-dimension heuristics.

title: Frobenius count in SL₂(ℤ/q) for the SL₂ form of ES
connection: Ore-type proofs count solutions of word equations via Σ_χ χ(g)/χ(1). The SL₂ form asks for γ = [[a, p],[c, d]] with a ≡ d ≡ −1 (mod c); reduced mod q this is a count of elements in a double-coset-type subset of SL₂(ℤ/q); its character expansion has nontrivial terms bounded by 1/χ(1) ~ 1/q.
why: Shows how much cancellation is available 'for free' in a nonabelian encoding (local information only, but with strong decay).
first_step: Compute for primes q the number of solutions mod q via characters of SL₂(F_q) and compare with the abelian (genus) expansion's error.
refs: Liebeck-O'Brien-Shalev-Tiep, The Ore conjecture, J. Eur. Math. Soc. 12 (2010) 939-1008

title: Wielandt-style orbit counting: a group action whose non-certificate orbits have size ≡ 0 (mod m)
connection: Wielandt proves Sylow existence because |X| = C(p^a m, p^a) ≢ 0 (mod p), so some orbit has size prime to p. ES: find a finite set X_p (e.g. 4-term or 'imprimitive' representations, or divisor configurations) with a group G (ℤ/3 permuting coordinates, S₃, or a dihedral group of moves) acting so that every orbit not containing a certificate has size divisible by m while |X_p| ≢ 0 (mod m).
why: Generalises the Zagier involution (m = 2) to larger groups where the needed congruence of |X_p| may be easier to establish.
first_step: Enumerate candidate (X_p, G) pairs for small p and check orbit-size divisibility; look for one where |X_p| mod m is given by a formula in p.

title: Non-lacunary semigroups of levels: multiplicative closure of 'working levels'
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity uses non-lacunarity of {2^a 3^b}. If level C works for p, does level C·k work for p for many k? (If d | 4Cp + 1 with d ≡ −1 mod 4C, then nothing obvious at level Ck.) Study whether the set of working levels for p is close to a multiplicative semigroup.
why: If working levels had semigroup structure, rigidity theorems for multiplicative semigroups could constrain failure.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁷ compute the set of working levels and test closure under multiplication by small k.

title: Thin-semigroup local-global with the ES constraint t ∈ 4ℤ ∪ (8ℤ − p): local obstructions?
connection: Bourgain–Kontorovich require knowing the local (congruence) obstructions of the semigroup before counting. Compute the reductions mod q of the ES-word set with the constraint on t (4ℤ for one branch, 8ℤ − p for the other, which depends on p!) and determine exactly which residues of p are locally admissible; check that only squares-related obstructions appear (T1-type).
why: The p-dependent constraint (8ℤ − p) is unusual for thin-orbit theory; its local analysis is a concrete, finite task.
first_step: For q ≤ 200 compute the set of p mod q (and mod 8q) hit by words with each constraint branch.

title: Large deviations of Euclid's algorithm at a fixed denominator (Hensley, Baladi–Vallée)
connection: The CF length of a/v is asymptotically Gaussian with mean ≍ log v (Heilbronn for the mean at fixed denominators; Hensley, Baladi–Vallée via transfer operators — reviewer repair: Baladi–Vallée average over denominators v ≤ N with rate O(1/√log N), not a fixed denominator). ES₅ (λ(p) ≤ 3) asks for an extreme left-tail event (length 3, prescribed shape). Large-deviation estimates for fixed p from the dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm would give lower bounds in exactly this quantifier order.
why: The dynamical analysis of Euclid's algorithm is 'every p' by construction (it averages over a, not p); the question is how far into the tail its estimates reach.
first_step: Find fixed-denominator large-deviation statements (Hensley's work on fixed-denominator Euclid statistics; check) beyond Baladi–Vallée's denominator-averaged ones; compare the reachable tail with length-3 events (count ≍ log²p out of p).

title: Triangle groups of covolume 2π(1 − 4/n)
connection: ES(n) for n ≥ 5 ⇔ there is a hyperbolic triangle group Δ(x,y,z) whose orbifold area is 2π(1 − 4/n), equivalently a hyperbolic triangle with angles π/x, π/y, π/z and area π(n−4)/n.
why: The covolume spectrum of Fuchsian groups is classically studied (Siegel's minimal covolume, signature theory). ES becomes 'every number of the form 2π(n−4)/n is a triangle-group covolume'.
first_step: Check whether 'areas of hyperbolic triangle orbifolds' as a set of rationals has been studied (search 'orbifold Euler characteristic triangle group which rationals'); list areas for arithmetic triangle groups.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0026] Search the literature for results on the set of covolumes of triangle groups, e.g. 'which rationals are 1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z'; check whether any density/representation theorem exists.
[analogues-0187] Explore: if ES(n₁) and ES(n₂) triangles glue along an edge, what Egyptian equation does the quadrilateral satisfy?

[free_opus-0415] Search literature for 'set of areas / Euler characteristics of triangle orbifolds' and 'which rationals are orbifold Euler characteristics of genus-0 three-point orbifolds'; record any density/representability theorem.

[free_opus-0424] Render the Coxeter triangle tessellations for a few ES solutions of 4/p (outreach) and check whether the 'arithmetic' triangle groups (Takeuchi's finite list) ever give ES certificates.
[signature-0431] Check whether 'which rationals are Euler characteristics of triangle orbifolds' appears in the orbifold literature, and test small p via tables of triangle groups with given area.
[upgrades-0229] Work out what Riemann–Hurwitz says for covers of S²(x,y,z) with χ = (4 − p)/p (index must be divisible by p); look for a moduli space whose nonemptiness is equivalent to ES(p).
refs: arXiv:2011.12940 (Chen, Nonabelian level structures, Nielsen equivalence, and Markoff triples, Ann. Math. 2024)

title: Riemann–Hurwitz integrality: a surface subgroup of Δ(x,y,z) of index d needs n | d(n − 4)
connection: For an ES solution, a torsion-free normal subgroup of index d in Δ(x,y,z) yields genus g with 2g − 2 = d(1 − 4/n). Hence n must divide d(n − 4); for prime n ≥ 5 this forces n | d.
why: Translates ES into 'Δ(x,y,z) has a finite quotient of order divisible by n with x, y, z element orders' — a group-theoretic existence statement where e.g. PSL₂(F_q) quotients (Macbeath) are classified.
first_step: For small n list ES triples and check whether PSL₂(F_p) is a quotient of Δ(x,y,z) (Macbeath's criterion); see if a uniform choice like PSL₂(F_p) suggests a construction.

title: Brieskorn links: ES solutions never give integral homology spheres
connection: The link of x^a + y^b + z^c is an integral homology sphere iff a, b, c are pairwise coprime. Pairwise coprime ES solutions are impossible (constraint-world item), so ES links always have non-trivial H₁.
why: Gives a topological invariant (H₁ of the link, related to gcds of the denominators) attached to every solution; the gcd skeleton of Type I/II solutions becomes the torsion of H₁.
first_step: Compute H₁ of Brieskorn links for ES triples of small p and compare with the Type I/II parameters.

title: Exact Seifert/pretzel form: ES(n) ⇔ a Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) with Euler number −4/n (double cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z))
connection: The Seifert space over S² with unnormalised invariants (x,1),(y,1),(z,1) has rational Euler number e = −(1/x + 1/y + 1/z) and |H₁| = xy + yz + zx. It is the double branched cover of the pretzel link P(x,y,z), with det P = xy + yz + zx. So ES(n) ⇔ some positive pretzel link P(x,y,z) has det = 4xyz/n ⇔ some such Seifert space has e = −4/n.
why: It is an exact translation of the original equation into 3-manifold/knot language. The fields have structure theorems for pretzel knots (sliceness, genus, Heegaard Floer) and for Seifert invariants, with n appearing as the Euler number.
first_step: Tabulate, for n < 200, the pretzel links P(x,y,z) realising ES solutions; check whether Type I/II solution families correspond to natural pretzel families (e.g. one strand dividing another) and whether T1 square classes relate to slice pretzel knots (Greene–Jabuka; det must be a square).
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0158] Check: a fibre-preserving d-fold cover of M multiplies e by a rational factor; derive which covers map ES(n) solutions to ES(n') solutions.
[analogues-0159] For ES triples of small p compute signature and Alexander polynomial of P(x,y,z); look for constraints that would forbid solutions at specific p.

[free_opus-0421] Check the sign conventions and the |H₁| formula for Seifert rational homology spheres; then compute linking forms of these M for ES solutions at odd squares vs primes and see whether T1 appears as a linking-form condition.

[translate-0025] Write H₁ and χ for Seifert spaces M(0; (x,β₁),(y,β₂),(z,β₃)); check whether ES(n) is equivalent to the existence of one with χ = 4/n − 1 and an extra homological condition with natural meaning (e.g. |H₁| ≡ 0 mod n).
refs: Greene–Jabuka, The slice-ribbon conjecture for 3-stranded pretzel knots (Amer. J. Math. 2011)

title: Star-shaped Dynkin trees T_{x,y,z}: det(Cartan) = xyz(1/x + 1/y + 1/z − 1)
connection: The tree T_{p,q,r} (arms with p, q, r vertices including the centre) has Cartan determinant pqr(1/p+1/q+1/r − 1) (E₈ = T_{2,3,5}: 1; E₆ = T_{2,3,3}: 3). ES ⇔ some T_{x,y,z} has n·det = xyz(4 − n), a hyperbolic lattice of discriminant xyz(n−4)/n.
why: Brings in lattice/root-system tools (discriminant groups, Vinberg reflectivity) and the recent weighted-star-tree classification of Torrente-Lujan.
first_step: Compute discriminant groups of T_{x,y,z} lattices for ES triples of small p; see whether they have a uniform structure (e.g. cyclic of order xyz(n−4)/n).

title: Weighted star trees with central weight k: determinant xyz(k − 3 + Σ 1/x_i) — ES with integer offset
connection: Torrente-Lujan allows central diagonal entry k; the determinant becomes xyz(k − 3 + 1/x + 1/y + 1/z) (k = 2 recovers xyz(Σ 1/x_i − 1); e.g. k = 3, arms (2,2,2) gives 12). Different k shift the target by integers, giving 'ES with integer offset'.
why: Integer offsets are trivial arithmetically but the matrix world might impose inertia/definiteness constraints that select ES-relevant triples.
first_step: Read arXiv:2605.23011 for the determinant formula with general k and record the induced Egyptian equation.

title: Arithmetic triangle groups (Takeuchi's 85) and ES triples
connection: Only finitely many triangle groups are arithmetic (Takeuchi). An ES triple (x,y,z) giving an arithmetic Δ would carry a quaternion algebra; for large n, ES triples are non-arithmetic.
why: A finite check: which n have an ES triple among Takeuchi's list; quaternion data might connect to the repo's quaternion forms.
first_step: Intersect Takeuchi's list with {(x,y,z) : 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n} and list the n obtained.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0169] List Takeuchi's 85 triples, compute 1/x+1/y+1/z, and find which equal 4/n.

title: Spherical / Euclidean / hyperbolic trichotomy as a 'phase diagram' of numerators
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z > 1 (spherical: the infinite family (2,2,r) plus finitely many others), = 1 (Euclidean: (3,3,3),(2,4,4),(2,3,6)), < 1 (hyperbolic). ES with 4/n < 1 sits in the hyperbolic regime; numerators m/n > 1 give the spherical lists.
why: The classification for sums > 1 (one infinite family plus a finite list) is the archetype of an 'Egyptian classification' theorem; ES is the infinite hyperbolic regime where no classification is possible but density is.
first_step: Record as context; check whether 'which rationals in (1, 3] are 3-term sums' (finite-ish lists per denominator) gives a useful contrast for heuristics.

title: Tessellations and Wythoff constructions: uniform tilings with vertex configurations from ES triples
connection: A triangle (π/x, π/y, π/z) tiles the hyperbolic plane; vertex/edge/face counts of Wythoff tilings depend on 1/x+1/y+1/z. ES triples give tilings with angle defect 2π·... proportional to (1 − 4/n).
why: Mostly a reformulation; potential value is visual/heuristic (e.g. counting tilings with given defect).
first_step: Low priority: note equivalence; compute angle defects of ES triangles for p ≤ 100.

title: Hypergeometric differential equations: exponent differences 1/x, 1/y, 1/z with Σ = 4/n
connection: Schwarz's list: the hypergeometric equation with exponent differences (λ, μ, ν) has monodromy a triangle group when they are reciprocals of integers; λ + μ + ν < 1 gives hyperbolic monodromy. ES ⇔ some Schwarz triangle with reciprocal angles has angle sum 4π/n.
why: Connects to monodromy/arithmetic of hypergeometric functions (Beukers–Heckman); ES triples give specific hypergeometric families whose arithmeticity could be tested.
first_step: Context; check whether any ES triple gives an arithmetic monodromy group (overlaps Takeuchi item).

title: Tropical ES: min(−v(x), −v(y), −v(z)) structure and Newton polytopes
connection: Tropicalizing 4xyz − n(xy + yz + zx) at a prime ℓ gives a tropical surface; ES solutions with given ℓ-adic valuations lie on cells of it. Over each ℓ | n the cell structure forces which denominators carry ℓ.
why: The tropical picture is exactly the Type I/II case split at ℓ = p; at other ℓ it describes the 'gcd skeleton'. Systematizing it gives a finite combinatorial classification of valuation patterns.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety of the ES surface for ℓ = 2 and ℓ = p and list all cells; match with Type I/II and with the 2-adic observations (m = 8, 4 | denominator).
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0098] Compute the tropical hypersurface of the Newton polytope of 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) (with n's valuation as a parameter) and plot where known solutions' (log x, log y, log z) fall.

title: Rademacher/Dedekind-sum reciprocity world for the triangle orbifold invariants
connection: Rho/eta invariants of Seifert spaces from ES triples are sums of Dedekind sums with reciprocity laws; T1 is a reciprocity phenomenon. Checking whether T1's congruence can be derived from Dedekind reciprocity applied to ES triples.
why: A second, topological derivation of T1 would show it is a genuine invariant-theoretic constraint and might suggest generalizations (other numerators, other square classes).
first_step: Compute Σ s(1, x_i) (or the Casson–Walker invariant) for ES triples at small p and look for congruences mod small numbers.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0352] Compute Σ s(1, x_i) mod small integers for ES triples at odd squares vs primes; look for a forced value.

title: Toric/polytope view: ES triples ↔ reflexive-like triangles with given lattice data
connection: A lattice triangle with vertices on axes at distances x, y, z (simplex with intercepts) defines the plane X/x + Y/y + Z/z = 1, which contains the diagonal point (t,t,t) iff Σ 1/x_i = 1/t. So ES ⇔ some plane with positive integer intercepts passes through (n/4, n/4, n/4).
why: Lattice-point/geometry-of-numbers view: find a lattice plane with positive integer intercepts through the diagonal point at height n/4. This is a 'plane through a point' problem amenable to geometry of numbers.
first_step: Formalize: planes with integer intercepts through (t,t,t), t = n/4; parametrize by normal vector (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) and relate to the repo's lattice forms.

title: Lattice-point/hyperbola methods (Dirichlet divisor problem) for fixed-p ES counts
connection: ES counts at fixed p are sums of divisor-counting functions over arithmetic progressions; the Dirichlet hyperbola method with exponent pairs gives error terms.
why: Comparing the main term ≍ log²p with error terms shows whether any pointwise statement is within reach of classical exponent-pair technology (likely not).
first_step: Count factor pairs of the fixed-x product equation in the required residue classes using divisor bounds and compare across x.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0249] Write the fixed-p count as a lattice-point count under a hyperbola with congruences and identify the error term size.
[signature-0461] Write the ES count as Σ_x #{d | (nx)² : d ≡ −nx mod (4x − n), d < nx} and check parity/symmetry under d ↔ (nx)²/d.

title: Hereditary/inductive world: ES(p) from ES of smaller primes via composition laws
connection: COMPOSITION_ES studies composition. A world where solutions compose (e.g. via Seifert-space covers or AP packings) would give induction: if ES(p) follows from ES(q) for smaller q dividing some p-tied integer, ES follows by strong induction.
why: An inductive mechanism is the classical way to prove 'for all p' statements; any composition law with the right divisibility closure would suffice.
first_step: Check COMPOSITION_ES.md for laws of the form ES(q) ⇒ ES(p) when q | f(p); search for f with q < p always available.

title: Lattice of solutions: the Z-span of solution vectors (1/x, 1/y, 1/z) as p varies
connection: For each p the solutions give rational vectors with coordinate sum 4/p. Their Z-span or the lattice generated by the denominators across p might show hidden linear relations (e.g. always containing a fixed vector).
why: A fixed vector in all solution spans would be a 'universal certificate' in disguise.
first_step: Compute for p < 2000 the lattice generated by (lcm/x, lcm/y, lcm/z) and look for invariants.

title: Catalog: Minkowski convex body theorem
connection: Minkowski convex body theorem ↔ ES as a small-count existence problem. Expected witnesses/n: ≥ 1 lattice point. Obstruction: —. Status: proved. Mechanism: volume.
why: Geometry-of-numbers existence; ES lattice reformulations exist (BALANCED_LATTICE.md).
first_step: None.

title: Transfer: hyperbolic lattice-point counting in log-size regions
connection: Type II solutions are integer points on a quadric-type variety in a region whose volume grows only like log² p; equidistribution theorems (Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak, Eskin–McMullen) need power-size regions.
why: Explains in a geometric language why ES sits below the 'counting with error term' regime; points to effective equidistribution in small regions as the needed input.
first_step: Identify an explicit quadric Q and region R_p with #(Q(ℤ) ∩ R_p) = R_II(p); compute vol(R_p).

title: U failures factor as products of small primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) and one larger factor
why: Composite U failures are driven by the composite structure (factors ≡ 3 mod 4 make n+v divisors in the needed class scarce?); 25305 contains 241 (least p ≡ 1 (4) with least QNR 7) — a weak link to pseudosquare-type hardness.
first_step: Test whether U-failure rate among n ≡ 1 (8) depends on the number of prime factors ≡ 3 (mod 4) of n; predict further failures beyond 10⁹ from that profile.

title: Sibling 4/n with denominators in an arithmetic progression or geometric constraints
connection: Solutions with y − x = z − y or y² = xz (geometric) are 'rigid' sub-families; their existence sets at primes are new exception sets.
why: Rigid families are where polynomial-identity constructions live; their failure sets indicate which residue classes each rigid family covers.
first_step: Add the two flags to the variant counter and list failures at primes ≤ 10⁵.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Distribution of x/p over all solutions (the 'x-profile')
connection: Histogram of x/p ∈ (1/4, 3/4] over all solutions at primes 10⁴–2·10⁵; expect mass near 1/4 (greedy) with a 1/(4x − p)-type law.
why: The x-profile is the density a sieve over x must reproduce; deviations (e.g. secondary peaks at x/p = 1/3, 1/2) show identity families.
first_step: Extend the count program to histogram x/p and y/p.

title: Balanced solutions (z ≤ 10x) frequency
connection: Fraction of primes with a solution having z/x ≤ C for C = 10, 100, 1000; BALANCED_LATTICE.md studies balanced points.
why: If balanced solutions exist for all large p with C fixed, geometry-of-numbers on the cubic surface (bounded-height points) would suffice — a strong statement to falsify cheaply.
first_step: Add a min z/x statistic to the count program and record its maximum over p ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Near-isosceles solutions: smallest y − x (or z − y) at p ≡ 1 (4)
connection: Since x = y is impossible at p ≡ 1 (4), the minimal gap y − x over solutions is a fingerprint of how close the hard class comes to the degenerate locus.
why: If the minimal gap is always small (bounded or ≪ log p), near-degenerate families might give uniform certificates.
first_step: Add min(y − x) and min(z − y) to the count program; tabulate at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 2·10⁵.

title: Primitive projective triples
connection: View denominator triples as rational points up to common scaling, with p recovered from their reciprocal sum.
why: Scaling explains why prime cases are central and may separate shape from arithmetic size.
first_step: Enumerate primitive triples with coordinates below 100 and sort the resulting reduced values of 4xyz/(xy+xz+yz).

title: Bilinear determinant encoding
connection: Represent uv−r as a two-by-two determinant and translate ES divisor conditions into determinant equations with congruences.
why: Determinants bring row operations and lattice bases into a directly arithmetic setting.
first_step: Write a residual factor-pair certificate as a determinant condition and list congruence-preserving row operations.

title: Lattice basis reduction for residues
connection: Encode simultaneous divisibility and smallness conditions as an integer lattice and use reduced bases to propose auxiliary parameters.
why: Short vectors can suggest candidates even without an existence theorem.
first_step: Build a two-constraint lattice for one residual factor search and compare reduced vectors with brute force.

title: Fundamental domain boundary crossings
connection: Follow a moving residue target through lattice fundamental domains as p changes and record when short representatives appear.
why: Boundary crossings may explain abrupt changes in the cheapest certificate.
first_step: Track nearest lattice representatives for consecutive admissible primes in one explicit two-variable model.

title: Ehrhart families of auxiliary polytopes
connection: When a parametrization reduces to linear inequalities and congruences, study its integer-point count as the bounds dilate.
why: Quasipolynomial counts can give exact finite-family information without addressing nonlinear cases automatically.
first_step: Isolate one linear parameter region and compute its first several dilation counts.

title: Inside-out polytopes for exclusions
connection: Represent linear positivity regions with forbidden congruence hyperplanes or boundary subspaces in a lifted lattice.
why: This separates the bulk feasible region from thin degeneracies.
first_step: For a small linear family, list forbidden hyperplanes and count remaining lattice points at low dilation.

title: Discrete Morse reductions
connection: Assign a combinatorial gradient to a bounded certificate complex and collapse redundant regions.
why: A reduced complex might isolate the essential obstructions to moving between certificate families.
first_step: Build a small complex from compatible local moves and test elementary collapses with explicit free-face checks.

title: Persistent topology of bounded searches
connection: Filter a point cloud of certificates by height and examine components and cycles as the cutoff grows.
why: Persistent features can suggest missing transformations; they are exploratory descriptors, not arithmetic obstructions.
first_step: For one p, compute only sparse graph-based persistence of certificate shapes at several height thresholds.

[translate-0279] Compute Vietoris–Rips persistence for the word clouds of 100 primes near 10⁶ vs 100 near-squares; compare barcodes.

title: Nerves of parametrization charts
connection: Construct the nerve whose vertices are exact parametrizations and whose simplices record shared certificates.
why: Intersections may expose a small core of identities linking otherwise separate approaches.
first_step: Compute pairwise and triple intersections for five small parametrization families over a finite prime sample.

title: Escape to the cusp
connection: Interpret unusually large minimal denominators as possible degeneration of an associated lattice basis.
why: This can distinguish missing certificates from certificates hidden in highly anisotropic regions.
first_step: For difficult bounded instances, compute successive minima of a relevant small lattice and compare them with denominator imbalance.

title: Stationary points of certificate cost
connection: Minimize smooth proxies such as log(xyz) on the real ES surface under specified denominator ordering and bounds.
why: Critical points indicate where an integer search should concentrate, not where integer solutions must exist.
first_step: Use Lagrange multipliers for one bounded cost and compare its minimizers with actual small certificates.

title: Hidden-number-style parameter recovery
connection: Treat partial information about modular products as a lattice recovery problem for an auxiliary parameter.
why: The analogy is meaningful only when the available information matches an explicit hidden-number instance.
first_step: Write a toy recovery problem with exact known high bits and compare its recovered parameters with valid certificates.

title: Motivic comparison as a bookkeeping lead
connection: Ask whether several auxiliary varieties share a common geometric decomposition that explains repeated finite-field count formulas.
why: A decomposition could transfer exact counting identities, but any motivic interpretation remains to be checked.
first_step: Compute point counts of two related charts over several small odd fields and seek an explicit cut-and-paste decomposition.

title: Finite-field incidence bounds
connection: Represent a reduced certificate relation as incidences between points and curves over a finite field.
why: Incidence geometry can estimate modular witness abundance, with integer lifting kept as a separate problem.
first_step: For the residual factor equation modulo q, identify the point and curve sets and count incidences directly for small q.

title: Hyperbolic lattice-point counting in a 'thin' cone: ES as a Selberg-pretrace positivity
connection: ES's Type II condition ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 is a 'determinant = 1' condition on a 2×2 integer matrix [[f, 2c], [2cd, f′]]... (up to normalization); counting such matrices with congruence constraints is hyperbolic lattice point counting.
why: Lattice-point problems in SL₂(ℤ) have error terms via spectral theory; the campaign's B3 says the main term is only log²p, but spectral *positivity* (not counting) might still apply to a cleverly weighted sum.
first_step: Verify exact matrix form: find integers such that det [[f, α],[β, f′]] = 1 encodes ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 (α β = 4c²dp); then check whether the congruence f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd is a Γ₀/Γ₁-type condition.

title: Topological-insulator-style 'bulk-boundary' invariant: Mordell classes as a bulk, squares as the boundary
connection: The 6 square classes mod 840 are the 'boundary' where polynomial identities fail; a ℤ/2 invariant (Brauer class) separates bulk from boundary. Bulk–boundary correspondence predicts protected 'edge states' — here, solutions that exist for a reason that only works away from squares.
why: Pure analogy, but it gives a design principle: look for mechanisms indexed by a ℤ/2-valued invariant that is nontrivial exactly on non-squares (e.g. a Jacobi symbol (p/m) that is +1 at squares).
first_step: List all ℤ/2 invariants of the form 'Jacobi symbol of p w.r.t. something determined by (C,d)' that are identically +1 when p is a square, and check which the known Type I/II identities use.

title: LLL on the 3-variable ES equation directly: find small solutions to 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) = 0 via Coppersmith bivariate
connection: After fixing x (≈ n/4 + small), the equation in (y,z) is a bivariate integer polynomial of bidegree (1,1): (4x − n)yz − nx(y+z) = 0 ⇒ ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x². So solutions are divisor pairs of n²x² in classes — Coppersmith's bivariate method finds small roots.
why: The factorisation ((4x−n)y − nx)((4x−n)z − nx) = n²x² is the classical two-term reduction; the 'small root' regime y,z ≤ n^{1+ε} may be exactly where solutions live. Quantify.
first_step: Check numerically: for p ≤ 10⁶, what is min over solutions of max(y,z)/p? Does a solution with max ≤ p^{3/2} always exist? (Relates to known bounds on denominators.)

title: Geometry of numbers: Minkowski's theorem on the 'Type II' lattice to force a divisor pair
connection: Type II: ff′ − 4c²dp = 1 with f ≡ f′ ≡ −1 mod 4cd. For fixed (c,d), the set {(f, f′)} is a congruence sublattice; Minkowski's theorem guarantees a nonzero lattice point in any convex body of volume 2^k det Λ; the hyperbola ff′ = 4c²dp + 1 is not convex, but regions between hyperbolas are.
why: Pigeonhole/Minkowski is the classic 'existence for every n' tool (two-squares theorem); it fails here because the target is a single hyperbola, but a 'union over (c,d)' body might have enough volume. Quantify.
first_step: For fixed p, compute the total 'volume' Σ_{(c,d) ≤ X} (area of the region 4c²dp < ff′ < 4c²dp + 2 inside the congruence conditions) vs the lattice determinant; see at which X Minkowski-type volume exceeds the threshold (expect: never by a polylog factor — document the gap).

title: Toric degenerations and Ehrhart counting of ES solutions in boxes
connection: Counting lattice points in polytopes defined by Type II inequalities ↔ Ehrhart quasi-polynomials.
why: The (★) count over a cut-off region is a lattice-point count in a hyperbolic region; Ehrhart theory with dilation p might give exact periodic formulas for partial counts.
first_step: Restrict to u ≤ U, B ≤ V and count solutions mod 4uB to p as function of p; check if it's a quasi-polynomial in p of bounded period.

title: Farey graph geodesics and ES as a 'triangle' in the Farey tessellation
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p ↔ mediants/Farey neighbours: Egyptian splitting a/b = 1/x + c/d occurs along Farey edges.
why: Hyperbolic geometry of the Farey graph might turn ES into a bounded-length path existence between two cusps — geometric group theory tools (Gromov hyperbolicity) apply.
first_step: Express each ES solution as a path in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 and record lengths/turn sequences for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Crystallography / Bravais lattices: 1/x+1/y+1/z as Miller-index relation
connection: Miller-index plane equations x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 ↔ the plane through (x,0,0),(0,y,0),(0,0,z) contains the point (p/4,p/4,p/4) ⟺ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some lattice plane with positive integer axis intercepts passes through (p/4)(1,1,1). Lattice-plane counting (geometry of numbers) might apply.
first_step: Use this: count lattice planes through q = (p/4)(1,1,1) with integer intercepts; relate to primitive vectors (1/x,1/y,1/z) scaled — check if this is a known equivalence to ET.

title: Factoring with hints: ES as 'find a factor of 4Cp+1 in a residue class' (Coppersmith known-MSB/LSB attacks)
connection: Coppersmith factors N given half the bits of a factor; ES wants a factor of N_C = 4Cp+1 ≡ −1 mod 4C — i.e. the low bits (mod 4C) of the factor are known.
why: Known-LSB factoring (factors in a prescribed class mod M with M ≥ N^{1/4}) is polynomial time via lattices; ES's modulus 4C is tiny relative to N^{1/4}, but summing over C gives many tries.
first_step: Quantify: for which C is 4C ≥ (4Cp+1)^{1/4}? (C ≥ p^{1/3}) — then Coppersmith decides existence of a factor ≡ −1 mod 4C exactly; check whether the large-C range alone has certificates often (data).

title: Lattice attacks on 'hidden number problem' as a model for finding u with p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1)
connection: HNP: recover hidden α from approximations of α·t mod q ↔ ES conditions as simultaneous approximations.
why: Cryptanalysis has fine-tuned lattice dimensions/bounds for such problems; reuse could design efficient certificate finders for huge p.
first_step: Write ES Type II as approximations of p/(4uC−1) to integers; try a BKZ-based search for certificates at p ~ 10^40 and compare yield with brute force.

title: Lattice of exponent vectors: ES certificate as short vector in a relation lattice
connection: Repo gon_lll_relation_lattice ↔ relation lattices among divisor classes.
why: Already explored in repo; listing for coverage. New angle: use LLL to find a subproduct with prescribed class AND size constraint simultaneously.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/gon_lll_relation_lattice.md; check whether the size constraint (d < √N) was included in the lattice.

title: Borsuk–Ulam / necklace splitting as existence via equivariant topology
connection: Necklace splitting existence via Borsuk–Ulam ↔ ES as fair division of something?
why: Curiosity; equivariant topology proves existence without construction (PPA-type).
first_step: Look for a ℤ/2-equivariant map whose zeros are ES certificates (e.g. using symmetry y ↔ z).

title: Knot theory / linking numbers: Legendre symbols as linking numbers of primes (arithmetic topology)
connection: Mazur–Morishita arithmetic topology: primes ↔ knots, Legendre symbol ↔ linking number mod 2, Rédei symbol ↔ Milnor triple linking ↔ T1 obstruction is a reciprocity (linking) statement.
why: If T1 is a 'linking number' obstruction, the prime case might be a 'link is not split' statement — Milnor invariants at higher order could give finer obstructions or non-obstructions.
first_step: Express the T1 obstruction as a Legendre-symbol identity and translate into linking numbers à la Morishita; check whether Rédei triple symbols appear in the 4-rank analogue.

title: Geometry: ES as a lattice point on a hyperboloid-like surface in 3D and Minkowski–Hlawka counts
connection: Positive solutions (x,y,z) lie on a smooth surface in ℝ³ (cubic) ↔ counting lattice points on surfaces near the asymptotic directions (where one coordinate dominates).
why: Lattice points on curved surfaces: counts ≍ area / curvature-weighted; ES surface's curvature degenerates at infinity — where solutions concentrate.
first_step: Compute the 'area' of the ES surface patch in the box [p/4, p²]³ weighted appropriately and compare with log² p — a geometric derivation of the main term.

title: Khinchine flatness theorem for convex pieces of the certificate region
connection: A convex body with no lattice points has bounded lattice width (Khinchine flatness). The hyperbolic certificate region splits into convex pieces, so if ES fails at p, every convex piece is lattice-free and thin in some lattice direction.
why: Flatness-type arguments are the geometry-of-numbers native way to derive structure from emptiness. Here 'thin in a direction' might contradict the known shape of the region.
first_step: For a fixed (u,C) box, the certificate set is a coset of a lattice of determinant ~ uC; apply flatness to decide when a box must contain a coset point (it must if box is large relative to modulus) — computes 'guaranteed' boxes and shows the tied-modulus problem.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0200] Take the region {(X,Y): XY ≈ tp+1, X ≡ Y ≡ −1 (t)} in the lattice of those congruences; compute convex pieces' widths and compare with flatness constants.

title: Dimension theory: Hausdorff dimension of p-adic limits of failing primes (if infinitely many)
connection: If infinitely many (★)-failures existed, their closure in Ẑ is a compact set ↔ its dimension measures 'how sterile'.
why: Gives a quantitative profinite object for (★) failures (which are known to exist: 14 ≤ 10¹⁰); compare with sterile set K.
first_step: Compute residues of the 14 (★)-failing primes mod small moduli and see whether they lie in a small profinite set (e.g. all squares mod 3·5·7·…).

title: Triangles with integer exradii and inradius n/4
connection: For any triangle 1/r = 1/r_a + 1/r_b + 1/r_c, and every positive triple (r_a,r_b,r_c) is realised by a unique triangle (Ravi substitution). So ES(n) ⇔ there is a triangle with integer exradii and inradius exactly n/4.
why: An exact, unrestricted Euclidean-geometry form. Triangle geometry has its own integrality theory (Heronian triangles, integer exradii), and a Heronian strengthening gives testable variants.
first_step: Verify the 'any positive exradii ⟹ triangle' claim; then compute, over ES solutions for p ≤ 10⁴, how often e₂(x,y,z) is a perfect square (rational semiperimeter) and search literature for 'integer exradii triangles'.
alt_first_steps: [translate-0028] Test the stronger variant 'exists a Heronian triangle with integer exradii and inradius n/4' for n ≤ 10⁴; if it holds broadly, rational parametrisations of Heronian triangles give new families.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Sangaku (Japanese temple geometry) problems with unit-fraction radius relations
connection: Many sangaku give relations like 1/√r = Σ 1/√r_i or 1/r = Σ 1/r_i for tangent circles ↔ ES as an integer-radius configuration.
why: Curiosity/outreach; a configuration with 1/r = 1/r1 + 1/r2 + 1/r3 among mutually tangent circles might connect ES to Descartes/Apollonian integrality.
first_step: Search sangaku collections (Fukagawa–Rothman 'Sacred Mathematics') for a three-reciprocal radius relation and check if it's Descartes-compatible.

title: Barvinok short generating functions for ES certificates up to height B
connection: Barvinok's algorithm encodes lattice points of rational polyhedra as short rational generating functions. ES certificates at fixed level C are lattice points in a union of polyhedra intersected with a hyperbola, which needs a polyhedral approximation.
why: Short generating functions allow evaluation of counts mod 2, character-weighted sums, etc., quickly. This is a computational-native route to exact sign sums.
first_step: Approximate the region by polyhedra (dyadic pieces), compute the Barvinok representation (LattE), and test evaluating weighted sign sums for p ~ 10⁶.

[tools-0274] Check whether, after fixing the divisor size range, the Type I certificate set at fixed (p,c,d) is a polytope ∩ lattice; compute its Barvinok series for small cases.

title: Weighted projective line: ES(★) ⟺ O(p) ≅ ω ⊗ π*O_{P¹}(4C) on the stacky curve P(u,B)
connection: On P(u,B) one has h⁰(O(n)) = N(n; u,B) (denumerant), ω = O(−u−B), and O(uB) = π*O(1) from the coarse P¹ ↔ p = 4C·uB − u − B is exactly deg(ω) + 4C·deg(π*O(1)).
why: Puts (★) into algebraic-geometry language where Riemann–Roch/Serre duality on stacky curves is the Popoviciu formula and the denumerant symmetry N(n)+N(g_t−n) = t is Serre duality. Type I might then correspond to stacky curves with three orbifold points — a uniform geometric home for both types.
first_step: Verify the Serre-duality derivation of N(n) + N(g_t − n) = t on P(u,B); then test whether Type I certificates correspond to line bundles of the form ω ⊗ (pullback) on P(a,b,c)-type stacky curves (three orbifold points).

title: Torus knots T(u,B): 2g(T(u,B)) = (u−1)(B−1) and the (★) relation p + 1 = 2g + (4C−1)uB
connection: The semigroup ⟨u,B⟩ is the semigroup of the plane-curve singularity x^u = y^B (link = torus knot); its conductor is 2g = (u−1)(B−1) ↔ (★): p = 4CuB − u − B ⟺ p + 1 − 2g(T(u,B)) = (4C − 1)uB.
why: Links (★) to singularity theory (Milnor number μ = 2g) and knot invariants (Alexander polynomial exponents = semigroup); speculative, but singularity theory has deformation/adjacency structures that might act on certificates.
first_step: Check the identity and ask whether the condition '(p + 1 − μ) ≡ 0 mod uB with quotient ≡ 3 mod 4' has a meaning for the Milnor fibre or for the Alexander polynomial evaluated at roots of unity.

title: Coppersmith lattice method to sample ES witnesses at C ≈ p^{1/4}–p^{1/2}
connection: Coppersmith–Howgrave-Graham–Nagaraj find divisors in a residue class for s > N^{1/4} (with more work). For ES levels C in [p^{1/4}, p^{1/2}] this is a non-brute-force witness finder.
why: Turns the search into a lattice-reduction problem; lattice structure could expose WHY witnesses exist (short vectors) — F31.
first_step: Implement the Lenstra/Coppersmith divisor search for N = 4Cp+1, r = −1, s = 4C at C ≈ p^{0.3}, p = 10¹⁵ primes; count hits vs. expectation.

title: Strong symmetric genus spectrum (May–Zimmerman: every value occurs) as a ∀g∃G sibling via triangle groups
connection: May–Zimmerman: there is a group of every strong symmetric genus. Proofs use explicit group families acting with triangle signatures; Riemann–Hurwitz ties genus to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z (see triangle-orbifold item). Shares F01, F12.
why: A solved ∀∃ statement whose witness lives in the same unit-fraction equation (via Riemann–Hurwitz) — possibly a source of explicit families (x,y,z) with constrained 1/x+1/y+1/z.
first_step: Read May–Zimmerman's construction and check which signatures (x,y,z) and areas arise; see if area (p−4)/p is ever forced.

title: Hurwitz 84(g−1) / the spectrum of 1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z: gaps near 0 vs ES's values (n−4)/n
connection: The set {1 − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z} has the minimum positive value 1/42 and a well-studied accumulation structure (Hurwitz). ES asks whether every (n−4)/n belongs to {1 − Σ1/x_i} (n ≥ 5).
why: The order structure of the triangle-group 'area spectrum' (it is well-ordered with known limit points) is classical; ES is a membership question for an explicit sequence in it.
first_step: Compute the area spectrum up to denominator 10⁶ and its intersection with {(n−4)/n}; visualise where the hard n sit in the spectrum.
